title: "Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/04-inspect-archive/lec.qmd) · [Weekly self-check](quiz.qmd)


## Which seedlings received the treatment?

A lab partner has sent a small archive containing measurements and sample
information. Before doing statistics, we need to establish what is in the
archive and which files belong to the treated samples. We will do this with
ordinary command-line utilities. The data are simulated for teaching.

The archive in this exercise is a **small separate practice dataset** with four
samples. It is not the 24-plant dataset we will analyse in R. A **manifest** is a
table describing which samples and files are present. Sample identifiers connect
the manifest to the measurements.

## Put the download in a known place

1. Download [lab-data.zip](../downloads/lab-data.zip) with your browser.
2. Locate the downloaded file in File Explorer or Finder.
3. In your terminal, run `cd ~/introcomputing-shell`, then `pwd`.
4. Open that folder graphically using `explorer.exe .` in local Ubuntu on Windows
   or `open .` on Mac.
5. **Copy the downloaded ZIP into this workspace using the file manager.**
   Do not assume your Windows browser downloaded it into Ubuntu's home folder.
6. Back in the terminal, run `ls`. Confirm that `lab-data.zip` appears.

On a remote computer, use the course's supported transfer route when available.
The browser's local download is not automatically a remote file.

## Look before extracting

From `~/introcomputing-shell`, run:

```bash
unzip -l lab-data.zip
```

The `-l` option lists archive contents without extracting them. Identify
`README.txt`, `samples.tsv`, and the `measurements` and `field-notes` folders.
There should be four measurement files, S01 through S04. The displayed sizes
and dates are information about the archive entries; do not type them.

Now extract:

```bash
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
ls
less README.txt
```

The `-d lab-data` option chooses the destination folder. Extraction creates
ordinary files you can open; it does not remove the ZIP. In `less`, use Space
to move down, arrow keys to move by lines, and **q** to quit and return to the
prompt. A short file may already fit on one screen.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Extraction asks whether to replace a file

You have probably extracted into the same destination before. Stop and inspect
the destination in the file manager. For this first run, choose a fresh destination
name if necessary and use that name in `cd`. Do not automatically agree to replace
files that may contain your work.
:::

## Read a table without changing it

Run:

```bash
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
```

`head -n 3` prints the first three lines. `wc -l` counts newline-terminated
lines. The supplied manifest has a header and four sample records, so the count
is **5**, not four biological samples. Tabs separate the columns in this TSV
(tab-separated values) file. A CSV uses commas instead.

The columns are `sample_id`, `treatment`, and `file`. Follow the file path for
sample S03:

```bash
head measurements/S03.csv
```

Before interpreting a number, use the README to find out what it measures and
which units were used. The filename locates measurements; it does not explain
their biological meaning by itself.

## Search the manifest with `grep`

Run:

```bash
grep -F treated samples.tsv
```

`grep` prints lines matching a search. `-F` asks for a **literal text** match,
so we do not need to learn pattern syntax. The supplied manifest should return
two lines, S03 and S04, labelled `treated`.

This is text search, not an understanding of table columns or experiments.
Searching for `treated` would also match `untreated` if that word were present.
Our prepared labels are `control` and `treated`; the header does not contain
the search word. Always inspect what a search actually selected.

## Save a search, then count its records

```bash
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
```

`>` redirects the output to a file instead of displaying it. **It replaces the
contents if that output file already exists.** Never use the input filename on
the right side here. `treated-samples.txt` is a new text extract; the original
`samples.tsv` remains unchanged. It has no header, because the header did not
match our search.

The vertical bar `|` is a **pipe**. It passes the matching lines from `grep`
to `wc -l`, which counts them. The result should be **2**. The pipe does not
need an intermediate saved file. Count lines only when lines really represent
the records you intend to count.

## Practical: preserve and organise a working copy

Still inside `lab-data`, run:

```bash
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
```

`cp` creates a copy; `mv` moves or renames an entry. Here only the practice copy
was renamed. Confirm that the original `samples.tsv` still exists. Both commands
can replace existing destinations, so check names before running them.

Use the file manager to create `observations.txt` inside `working`. Record:
how many sample records there are, which two received treatment, and which
measurement file you would open for S04. Add the distinction between the five
manifest lines and the four samples.

## A first look at the remote computer

The teacher will demonstrate [SSH and remote desktop](../intro/remote-linux.qmd).
SSH gives a terminal on another computer. A remote desktop gives a graphical
workspace there. In either case, saved files can be on that other computer,
even while your laptop displays the session.

When account details are available, follow the supplied instructions and try
`pwd` and `ls` remotely. State aloud: “This command runs on ___; this path is
on ___.” If accounts are not ready, continue the local practical. Do not guess
a login address.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Did `grep` change the manifest? Why does `wc -l` sometimes count a header?

`grep` reads the file; redirection saved its output separately. `wc -l` counts
lines, not their meaning. The full manifest includes a header, while our saved
matching lines do not. We must know the file's structure to interpret the count.
:::

**Save today:** `treated-samples.txt`, `working/manifest-practice.tsv`, and
`working/observations.txt` in the extracted `lab-data` folder. Be able to show
where the untouched archive and manifest are located.
